summary: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP). It describes managed objects that let network management tools monitor PCEP sessions between a path computation client and a path computation element, or between two such elements.

eli5.summary: Routers sometimes ask a helper computer to plan their routes. This document is a list of dials and meters that lets people look at how those conversations are going.

questions: how to monitor pcep sessions with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let operators watch PCEP sessions between path computation clients and elements.

tldr.problem: Operators running PCEP, the protocol routers use to ask a Path Computation Element for routes, had no standard way to monitor local entities, peers and sessions through network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7420 defines the PCE-PCEP-MIB module with three read-only tables (entities, peers, sessions), six notifications, and one writable object that throttles the notification rate.
tldr.outcome: A standard SNMP view of PCEP configuration, state and message counters. It covers only the PCEP base protocol, not extensions.

today: RFC 7420 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers the PCEP base protocol of RFC 5440 only, not extensions.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes a network path from a network graph and constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) can ask a PCE for paths. The protocol between them is PCEP, defined in RFC 5440, which carries path computation requests, replies and notifications in the context of MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering.

This memo defines a MIB module for monitoring PCEP interactions between a PCC and a PCE, or between two PCEs. It covers the PCEP base protocol of RFC 5440 only. Extensions to the base protocol are out of scope. Monitoring of the underlying protocols is also out of scope, since they have their own MIB objects.
sections.eli5: When routers ask a helper to plan routes, someone should be able to check how the conversation is going. This document defines the dashboard for that.

sections.title: SNMP and the SMI Framework
sections.content:
MIB objects are generally reached through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are defined with the Structure of Management Information. This module is written in SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580). The overview of the management framework is in RFC 3410.

The module imports the InetAddressType and InetAddress textual conventions from the INET-ADDRESS-MIB of RFC 4001. It sits at { mib-2 227 } under the name pcePcepMIB.
sections.eli5: SNMP is the standard way to ask a device for its numbers. The MIB is the menu of numbers you may ask for.

sections.title: Three Tables Linked by Index
sections.content:
The module holds local entity status, peer information, session information, and notifications. Everything is read-only except pcePcepNotificationsMaxRate.

  • pcePcepEntityTable: one row per local PCEP entity. There can be several, for example a router split into virtual routers each with its own PCC, or a PCE front-ending a cluster reached through different IP addresses. Each row holds current status and running configuration, and is indexed by pcePcepEntityIndex.
  • pcePcepPeerTable: one row per known peer, indexed by entity index, address type and address. A peer is identified by its IP address, so a speaker with several addresses looks like several peers. Rows persist when no session exists, and statistics aggregate all successive sessions. An implementation MAY discard a row only if no session exists to that peer.
  • pcePcepSessTable: one row per current session, with the running session configuration, identifiers and statistics for that session only. It adds pcePcepSessInitiator to the index.

RFC 5440 forbids more than one active session between a pair of entities. During session establishment, though, two rows can exist briefly, one initiated by each side. When either reaches an active state, the other is discarded. This is why the initiator is part of the session index.
sections.eli5: There are three lists: who I am, who I talk to, and the talks happening right now. A number in each row links it back to the other lists.

sections.title: Entity Configuration and Timers
sections.content:
The entity table exposes the configuration a PCEP entity runs with: administrative and operational status (up, down, going up, going down, failed, failed permanently), its address, and a family of timers in seconds.

  • Connection setup: pcePcepEntityConnectTimer (how long to wait for a TCP connection), pcePcepEntityConnectMaxRetry, and initial and maximum backoff timers for retrying failed setups.
  • Session start: an open wait timer for the Open message, and a keep wait timer for a Keepalive or PCErr after Open.
  • Liveness: the Keepalive and DeadTimer values the entity proposes in its Open message, plus minimum and maximum values it accepts when negotiation is allowed. Actual values are negotiated per RFC 5440 and appear in the session table.
  • Requests: a request timer (maximum wait for a reply to a PCReq) and a SyncTimer for synchronized requests that use the SVEC object. If not all of them arrive in time, a protocol error is triggered and the PCE MUST cancel the whole set.
  • Limits: maximum sessions, and the maximum unrecognized requests, replies and unknown messages accepted per minute before a session is terminated.
sections.eli5: These are the stopwatches and limits: how long to wait for a connection, how often to say hello, and how many strange messages to put up with before hanging up.

sections.title: Peer and Session Statistics
sections.content:
Peers and sessions carry matching sets of counters. The peer table counts across all sessions to that peer, and the session table counts the current session only. Both include sent and received counts of PCReq, PCRep, PCErr, PCNtf and Keepalive messages, unknown and corrupt messages, requests, SVEC objects, and the outcome of requests (pending replies, ERO received or sent, no path, cancel, error, timeout). Response times are given as average, low-water mark and high-water mark in milliseconds.

Peer rows also record the peer role (unknown, PCC, PCE or both), session setup successes and failures, and sysUpTime stamps for the last success and failure. A discontinuity time says when the statistics were last reset.

Session rows add the session state: tcpPending, openWait, keepWait or sessionUp. The idle state has no row. They also show local and remote session IDs, the agreed Keepalive and DeadTimer values, the remaining Keepalive hold time, and overload flags and times for the local entity and the peer.
sections.eli5: Counters work like a scoreboard: how many questions asked, how many answers back, how many errors, and how fast the answers came.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
Six notifications report session changes: pcePcepSessUp, pcePcepSessDown, pcePcepSessLocalOverload, pcePcepSessLocalOverloadClear, pcePcepSessPeerOverload and pcePcepSessPeerOverloadClear. The overload pair covers the local entity sending, or the peer sending, an overload or overload-cleared PCNtf on a session.

The one writable object, pcePcepNotificationsMaxRate, sets the maximum number of notifications issued per second. If events come faster, the implementation may drop notifications or queue them. A value of zero means no notifications are emitted and all are discarded rather than queued.
sections.eli5: The module can ring a bell when a conversation starts, stops, or gets too busy. A volume knob limits how often the bell may ring.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The writable pcePcepNotificationsMaxRate could be abused to silence notifications or to flood the management agent. Even the readable objects may be sensitive, since together they reveal how many path computation requests and replies occur and some aspects of the network's configuration.

Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features. Those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy using the User-based Security Model (RFC 3414) with the AES cipher (RFC 3826). They MAY also support the Transport Security Model (RFC 5591) over SSH or TLS/DTLS. Deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The numbers show how busy the network is, so only the right people should be allowed to read them. The volume knob must be locked.
